key_claims: Women who used estrogen-only hormone therapy later in life had lower odds of a dementia diagnosis.
Hormone therapy use was associated with 35% lower odds of showing signs of Alzheimer's disease at autopsy.
Among women who used hormone therapy, 18% showed no signs of Alzheimer's disease at autopsy, compared to 10% of non-users.
Biomarker tests suggested less amyloid buildup among hormone therapy users.
Hormone therapy use was associated with 39% lower odds of receiving a clinical dementia diagnosis.
Women who used hormone therapy were less likely to show memory problems or declines in daily functioning.
limitations: The study shows an association, not causation.
Participants used hormone therapy decades ago, with timing and type differing from current practice.
The average age of hormone therapy users was 70, whereas current practice typically starts in late 40s to early 50s.
The study focused only on estrogen-only therapy, not combined therapy.
what_not_to_say: Hormone therapy is recommended for brain health.
Estrogen-only therapy is safe for all women.
The results apply to current hormone therapy practices.
